features.headline: Karabell's notebook: Harden's declining role, Garland's TOs, a rookie to watch
features.desc: Eric Karabell empties out the notebook with all that he's noticing around the NBA and what it means for fantasy.
body: It's easy to claim otherwise today, but there was little indication Cleveland Cavaliers PG/SG James Harden would suddenly become a fantasy disappointment this season.
After all, Harden was terrific last season, averaging 43.5 ESPN fantasy points per game. Only 16 players scored more. Harden was 36 years old.

Is there really much difference between being 36 and 37 years old? (Guess I will find out in a few years when I turn 37, lol.) Harden may not have deserved a second-round slot in ESPN average live drafts, but there was regression built into projections and he fell to Round 4.

Harden is 11 games into the season and he's not performing as a top 50 fantasy option, certainly not yet anyway at 29.1 fantasy points per game, and many are whispering that this is the end of his time as a top point guard.
It is fine if Immanuel Quickley, Fred VanVleet or Coby White average 15.3 PPG, 4.8 RPG and only 5.7 APG, but certainly not if Harden does so.
Perhaps we didn't expect quite another 20.5 PPG, 4.8 RPG and 7.7 APG (his numbers in 26 games with the Cavaliers after the LA Clippers trade), but the current numbers are just not cool.

Is it reasonable to ask if this is all we're going to get this season? Perhaps it is, but there is a bigger picture going on with Cleveland. Harden has only 13 assists and nine turnovers in his past three outings, only one of them a win (over the Philadelphia 76ers, of course).
He won't shoot a ghastly 36.4% from the field for long, but watching Harden and his missing usage it is clear he is more willing to defer shots and in directing the offense.

features.headline: Gibbs, Allen, JSN and more Knockout league pickups for Week 10
features.desc: As the number of teams shrink, the number of stars available in Knockout leagues grows. Here are the ones to get.
body: Ten weeks in — and with nine teams remaining in full-season Knockout leagues — the strategy shifts. Weekly upside is becoming increasingly important, as rosters become ever-richer in talent.
Aiming only for statistical floor is no longer getting it done quite as effectively. You need those big scores in order to stay afloat now.

Additionally, FAB (Free Agent Budget) funds are shrinking, perhaps dramatically in your league. Take our two in-house Knockout leagues, for example. In one league, 36% of collective FAB funds remain. In the other, it's 41%. Among those 18 managers, eight have less than 30% remaining.
If you're in a good position in terms of FAB, we've reached the stage where you're now in command of the free-agent market.
Bully your competition for top free agents, examining likely competitors for newly available superstars and strategizing your bids dependent upon their resources.
Pinpoint ideal times to acquire the superstars you need, rather than tossing FAB at each and every superstar who comes available.

That's why the FAB recommendations in this space in each coming week will be exactly that: Recommendations. If you need to open your FAB wallet wider to get the player you need, do it. If your competition won't be as aggressive in pursuit of a specific player or position, hold back.

features.headline: As Jaylen Brown faces the Celtics for the first time, familiar questions linger
features.desc: Jaylen Brown and the Philadelphia 76ers host Jayson Tatum and the Boston Celtics on Tuesday night.
body: FOR MUCH OF his decade-long career with the Boston Celtics, Jaylen Brown spent time answering questions about his role.
Critics wondered whether he and Jayson Tatum could coexist, speculated about whose team it was. Both players, their teammates and coaches were aware of the narrative.
"The media wants to kind of sometimes write the story that pulls us apart," Brown said in 2021. "But we talk a lot. We don't let it bother us."
So as Brown — now a Philadelphia 76er after Boston traded him this offseason — sat at Sixers media day a month ago, a reporter asked him: "Do you guys know who the alpha is?"
There were years of frustration loaded into Brown's smirk and two-word response: "Next question."
Four months into his Sixers tenure, Brown has again fielded questions about his relationship with his former running mate in Boston, partly because of a social media firestorm Brown started.
It has led to back-and-forth comments between Brown and Tatum, and a report from NBC Sports and Celtics TV analyst Brian Scalabrine about Brown's "demands" and "trade request" in Boston.
Scalabrine later walked back his comments about Brown asking for a trade.
A source with knowledge of the situation told ESPN that there was no truth to the report.
Instead, the source said, Brown discovered his former team had tried — and failed — to trade him to the Milwaukee Bucks while he was on vacation over the summer.
The one thing Brown did ask for, the source said, was to be involved in the process of where he was traded. The Celtics ignored the request and sent him 300 miles southwest to Philadelphia.

features.headline: Breaking down the CFP race for three conferences after Week 10
features.desc: Before making a futures prediction after Week 10, let's look at three paths to conference championships.
body: We're entering Week 11 of the college football season, and yet, somehow less time means more questions. Nobody seems to know what to do with the Heisman, and I'm not seeing a price worth chasing right now.
For the record, Notre Dame QB CJ Carr (+220), Miami QB Darian Mensah (+250) and Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith (+280) are the three favorites.
The national title board hasn't moved enough to change my mind, either. So, let's look elsewhere.
Who will make the playoff? Who will win their conference? Between the remaining schedules and tiebreakers, there's plenty to sort through before we put money on any of it.

I went into the MAC thinking 7-2 Ohio might be the play. The Bobcats are undefeated in conference play, host Toledo (7-2 overall, 4-1 MAC) in Week 13 and boom: +295 to win it. There's something there.
But then I looked at how those teams match up, and Toledo's defense kept getting in the way. Ohio wants to run. Toledo is really good at stopping it, and it also has a much better passing game.
So now I'm looking at Ohio's bigger payout and asking whether I actually like the matchup or just the number.

Toledo at +146 isn't exactly giving us some huge discount. Western Michigan (6-3, 4-1 MAC) has a manageable schedule left, but I don't trust its offense as much. I can make a case for all three getting to the championship game. I'm less interested in paying these prices to find out which one does.

Memphis (7-2, 4-1 AAC) was the team I kept looking at in the American. I like Marcus Stokes and the passing game. I trust the Tigers' pass defense more than North Texas' or UTSA's. But Memphis still has to go to South Florida and Navy.

features.headline: The historic (and absurd) longevity of Steph Curry and Kevin Durant
features.desc: More than 10 years after briefly joining forces, Steph and KD remain near the top of their games at 38. How long can each legend keep this up?
body: When Stephen Curry and Kevin Durant teamed up a decade ago, their union created perhaps the most lethal scoring duo in NBA history and threatened to serve as the foundation of a dynasty that might have rivaled Michael Jordan's Chicago Bulls.
Curry and Durant were both former MVPs and scoring champions in their primes at 28 years old when they began their first title chase together in 2016-17.
As the Golden State Warriors raced out to a 20-3 start that fall, they were so thoroughly dominant that critics quickly deemed the pairing "unfair."

There have been two key developments since those halcyon early days: The Curry and Durant partnership disbanded quicker than anyone could have expected, while Curry and Durant (both now 38) have managed to sustain elite play much longer than anyone anticipated.

The first point is well-worn. After two championships and a torn Achilles, the nomadic Durant left the Bay Area to start fresh with the Brooklyn Nets. Meanwhile, Curry has become one of the NBA's all-time single-franchise icons.

The second point has been obscured by LeBron James' record-setting longevity. As James has rewritten the record books and kept playing into his 40s, Curry and Durant have prospered late in their respective careers like few superstars before them.

With Curry's Warriors and Durant's Houston Rockets set to face off Wednesday for the first time this season (9:30 p.m. ET, ESPN) let's take a moment to appreciate their remarkable staying power a full decade after they started torching the league as teammates.

features.headline: Who has won MLB Rookie of the Year? All-time winners list
features.desc: MLB's Rookie of the Year award is presented to the best rookies of the American and National League. Check out the full list of winners by year.
body: In 1947 and 1948, the Rookie of the Year was given to Major League Baseball's top rookie-eligible player. Since 1949, the award has been presented to a player in the American League and National League.
The Baseball Writers' Association of America votes on the award at the end of each season and before the start of the postseason.

Before 1957, voters used their own judgment to determine which players were considered rookies. After 1957, players were considered rookies if they had fewer than 75 at-bats or 45 innings pitched prior to the season.

This was later changed to 90 at-bats, 45 innings pitched or 45 days of MLB service time. In 1971, the mark was adjusted to 130 at-bats, 50 innings pitched or 45 days of non-September service time. That remains the standard today.
Jackie Robinson was MLB's first Rookie of the Year in 1947. Robinson hit.297 with 12 home runs, 31 doubles, five triples, 48 RBIs and 29 stolen bases for the Brooklyn Dodgers.
The award has been named the Jackie Robinson Award since 1987, the 40th anniversary of Robinson breaking the league's color barrier.

In 2026, Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers won the award for the American League, while Sal Stewart of the Cincinnati Reds won it for the National League. Here's a look at every rookie who has won the Jackie Robinson Award:
2023: Gunnar Henderson (AL), Corbin Carroll (NL)
2022: Julio Rodriguez (AL), Michael Harris II (NL)
2021: Randy Arozarena (AL), Jonathan India (NL)
2018: Shohei Ohtani (AL), Ronald Acuna Jr. (NL)
